planting.note: Fall-sow seed outdoors for natural cold-moist stratification over winter; germinates the following spring.

directions: Yellow pimpernel produces loose, airy umbels of tiny chartreuse-yellow flowers from late spring into early summer, rising above smooth blue-green foliage that gives off a faint anise scent when bruised. Unlike most members of the carrot family, which demand full sun, this eastern and midwestern woodland native thrives at the dappled edge of deciduous forest and on rocky, open slopes from Quebec and Ontario south to Georgia and Texas. Its small flowers draw an unusually broad crowd of pollinators, including sweat bees, wasps, hoverflies, and beetles, while the foliage feeds black swallowtail and Ozark swallowtail caterpillars. Give it dry to medium, well-drained soil in part shade to light sun; once established it needs little care and self-sows modestly along woodland paths.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery plugs in moist, humus-rich soil in shade; spreads by rhizome to form loose colonies.

directions: Stream violet carpets moist Pacific Northwest forest floors and streambanks with heart-shaped leaves and small, deep-yellow, purple-veined flowers from early spring through midsummer. Native from Alaska and British Columbia south through the Cascades and Sierra Nevada into California, it is one of the few true shade-loving violets of the western understory, spreading gently by rhizome beneath conifers and bigleaf maples. Bumblebees and other native bees work the nectar spur while the lower petal serves as a landing platform, and the foliage hosts fritillary butterfly caterpillars. It wants consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade and resents summer drought.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in consistently moist, part-shaded soil; spreads slowly by rhizome into patches.

directions: Cooley's hedge-nettle sends up tall, square mint-family stems topped with whorls of magenta-pink tubular flowers through mid- to late summer, standing out as one of the showiest nectar sources in Pacific Northwest wetland thickets and shaded forest openings. Despite the name, it is not a true nettle and does not sting; crushed foliage releases a pungent, resinous scent. Rufous and other hummingbirds are frequent visitors to the tubular blooms, alongside bumblebees and long-tongued bees, making it a reliable late-season hummingbird plant in rain gardens and streamside plantings from coastal Alaska to northern California. It spreads slowly by rhizome in consistently moist to wet, part-shaded soil and tolerates periodic flooding.

planting.note: Fall-sow or cold-stratify seed; also propagated readily by dividing established clumps in spring.

directions: Richardson's geranium bears white to very pale pink flowers with fine purple veining from early to late summer, held above deeply lobed leaves along shaded streambanks and moist forest openings of the Rocky Mountains and intermountain West, from British Columbia and Alberta south to Arizona and New Mexico. It is a reliable nectar source for native bees, syrphid flies, and small butterflies at mid to high elevations, often blooming later in the season than many other woodland perennials. Site it in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in part shade along a woodland edge, streambank, or seasonally damp meadow margin where it forms loose, long-lived clumps.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed for natural cold stratification, or divide clumps in early spring; prefers cool, humusy soil.

directions: Yellow columbine nods pale lemon-yellow flowers with long, elegant nectar spurs from late spring into midsummer, growing in subalpine meadows, open conifer forest, and rocky slopes of the Rocky Mountains and interior Pacific Northwest, from Utah and Wyoming north into British Columbia and Alberta. Its deep spurs are tailored to hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees, while shorter-tongued bees collect pollen from the open face of the flower. Site it in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to morning sun; it is naturally adapted to short, cool growing seasons and benefits from afternoon shade in warmer, lower-elevation gardens.
